newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Medical equipment maker NESS seeks Nasdaq listing.
newsitem.headline: Medical equipment maker NESS seeks Nasdaq listing.

text.p: Medical equipment maker NESS has filed a prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and company officials estimate an initial public offering on Nasdaq could be made in November.
"We are currently revising the prospectus and will refile soon," said Avi Kerbs, president and chief executive of Teuza, a venture capital fund that owns 40 percent of Israel's NESS.
He said a U.S. investment house would act as underwriter but he declined to name the firm.
Sources involved in the offering said they did not believe the current political tensions sparked by clashes between Israelis and Palestinians would affect or delay the offering.

Kerbs said, however, that NESS was still weighing the option of delaying the offering by a year, when the company would have a firm sales record and therefore go public at a higher valuation. Kerbs declined to estimate NESS's current valuation but said the underwriter has estimated that in a year's time NESS could be valued at $60 million.
NESS hopes to raise between $5 million and $10 million in the IPO. The company needs $3 million in the coming year, mainly for marketing purposes, Kerbs said.

NESS, or Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Systems Ltd, makes a device called the Handmaster, which restores functional use of the hand in quadriplegics and stroke victims. Unlike other systems developed in the United States and Japan, the Handmaster does not have to be surgically implanted.
A month ago NESS received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to market its device, which is expected to sell for $3,000.
The U.S. Veterans' Administration has decided to purchase the Handmaster on a trial basis though marketing in the United States has not yet begun.
NESS has started selling its device in Israel and Europe as well. But it is now focussing on an upgraded version of the Handmaster, expected to come to market in early 1997.
NESS has also been approached by investment houses interested in underwriting an offering in Canada and London, Kerbs said. "But we prefer Nasdaq," he added.
